title: Fashion Basics & Clothing Alterations
subtitle: Read fit, alter bodices, trousers, sleeves, necklines and gowns accurately, restyle old garments and price every job by the time it really takes.
description: A practical alterations course for women who already sew basic seams and hems. You will learn to read fit and ease, run a proper fitting, calculate exactly how much a garment can be taken in or let out, and carry out the alterations clients ask for most, from tapered trousers to lined aso-ebi gowns. The course ends with restyling projects and a working system for intake, scheduling and time-based pricing.
outcomes: Diagnose fit problems from ease measurements and drag lines and write precise alteration instructions
Run a respectful fitting, pin from the top down and mark level hems
Calculate take-in and let-out amounts using the doubling rule and a seam inventory
Alter bodices, waistbands, trouser legs, sleeves, necklines and lined gown hems in the correct order
Restyle an old garment after checking fabric yield and agreeing a written brief
Run an alteration counter and price jobs from timed minutes, difficulty and materials
audience: Women who can already use a sewing machine and sew simple seams and hems, and want to earn from alterations and restyling.
tools: Sewing machine with zipper foot (invisible zip foot helpful)
Tape measure, short ruler or seam gauge, metre rule
Tailor's chalk, pins, safety pins and a seam ripper
Iron, ironing board and pressing cloth
Full-length mirror and a private fitting corner
Notebook or phone for fitting cards, job slips and timing

modules.title: Seeing Fit Like an Alterations Specialist
modules.overview: Before you touch a seam ripper you must be able to look at a client in a garment and say exactly what is wrong, why, and whether it can be fixed. This module teaches you to read fit and ease, run a calm and accurate fitting, and give honest style advice about what an alteration will and will not achieve.

lessons.title: Reading fit: ease, drag lines and the five signs of a good fit
objectives: Explain the difference between wearing ease and design ease
Calculate the ease in a garment from a body measurement and a garment measurement
Read pulling, bagging and drag lines and name the area causing them
Decide whether a fit problem needs taking in, letting out or no change at all

blocks.text: Most alteration customers walk in with a feeling, not a diagnosis: "it is not sitting well", "it is too tight here", "it looks old". Your first job is to turn that feeling into a clear, measurable problem. To do that you need two ideas: **ease** and **drag lines**. With these two ideas you can explain almost every fitting problem you will meet on blouses, gowns, skirts and trousers.

blocks.name: trying-on-clothes
blocks.alt: A woman trying on clothes in front of a mirror
blocks.caption: Every alteration starts with the client wearing the garment while you look carefully at how it sits.

blocks.text: Ease: the room between the body and the cloth

**Ease** is the difference between the body measurement and the garment measurement at the same place. If a client's bust is 96 cm and the blouse measures 104 cm around the bust, the blouse has 8 cm of ease. Ease comes in two kinds. **Wearing ease** is the minimum room needed to breathe, sit, bend and raise the arms. **Design ease** is extra room the designer added on purpose to create a style, such as a loose boubou or a flowing kaftan.

Sewing references commonly quote wearing ease of roughly 5 to 6.5 cm at the bust, about 2.5 cm at the waist and about 5 to 7.5 cm at the hip for a fitted woven garment. Treat these as starting guides, not laws. Stretch fabrics need less ease, sometimes none. Evening wear that is worn standing for a short time can be closer than an office dress worn for nine hours. Always ask the client how she will wear the garment.

head: Fit category
What it looks like
Typical garments
rows: Follows the body, very little room beyond wearing ease
Corset lace gowns, mermaid skirts, stretch tops
Shows the body shape with comfortable room
Office dresses, fitted skirts and blouses
Skims the body, waist only lightly shaped
Plenty of design ease, shape comes from the cloth

blocks.title: Never remove design ease by accident
blocks.text: A client who says her kaftan is "too big" may simply be used to fitted clothes. If you take all the design ease out of a kaftan, it stops being a kaftan and the fabric will pull at the hips when she sits. Ask: does she want it to fit more closely, or does she want a different style?
Drag lines: the garment is telling you where the problem is
A **drag line** is a fold or wrinkle that forms because the fabric is being pulled or has too much room. The direction of the line points towards the cause. Learn to read three patterns.

items: **Pulling lines (tight):** fine wrinkles that stretch across the body, like rays. Horizontal lines across the hips of a skirt mean the hip is too tight. Lines pointing from the bust to the armhole can mean too little room at the bust.

**Bagging folds (loose):** soft, deep folds that hang. Vertical folds at the back waist of a dress mean there is too much width there. A pool of fabric above the waist at the back often means the back is too long for the client.

**Diagonal drag lines:** lines running at an angle usually point to the part of the body that needs more or less length or width, for example lines running from the neck down to the armhole can mean the shoulders are sloping more than the garment allows.

blocks.title: Diagnosing a fit problem
items: Client wears the garment
Look for drag lines
Measure body and garment
Work out the ease
Choose change or no change
blocks.caption: Look first, then measure, then decide; never pin before you understand the cause.

blocks.text: The five signs of a good fit

items: **Shoulder seams** sit on top of the shoulder and end at the shoulder bone, not down the arm (unless the style is a dropped shoulder).
**Side seams** hang straight down, at right angles to the floor, without swinging forward or back.
**Waistline** of a fitted garment sits at the natural waist, and the hem is level all round when the client stands relaxed.
**No pulling or bagging** at bust, back, hips or seat when she stands, and she can sit and raise her arms without strain.
**Closures lie flat:** zips do not ripple, buttons do not gape between the buttonholes.

blocks.title: Worked example: is this office dress too big or just loose?
blocks.context: For example, Halima, a bank officer in Kaduna, brings a ready-made fitted dress. She says it "hangs like a sack" at the waist but feels fine elsewhere. You measure her and then measure the dress laid flat, doubling the flat width.
steps: Bust: body 96 cm, dress 102 cm. Ease = 102 - 96 = 6 cm. That is within normal wearing ease, so leave the bust alone.
Waist: body 80 cm, dress 98 cm. Ease = 98 - 80 = 18 cm. Far more than the 2.5 cm guide and more than a fitted style needs.
Hip: body 104 cm, dress 110 cm. Ease = 110 - 104 = 6 cm, comfortable for sitting at a desk.

She wants a fitted look but must sit all day, so you agree a waist ease of about 4 cm. Target waist = 80 + 4 = 84 cm, so 98 - 84 = 14 cm must be removed at the waist, tapering to nothing at bust and hip.
blocks.result: The problem is only the waist. You write "remove 14 cm at waist, taper to 0 at bust and hip" on her job card, instead of the vague note "take in dress".

blocks.title: Measure the garment correctly
blocks.text: Lay the garment flat, close the zip or buttons, smooth it without stretching and measure straight across from fold to fold. Double that number to get the full circumference. Measure stretch fabrics relaxed, never pulled.

Some fit problems cannot be solved by an alteration at all. If a dress is too short in the bodice so the waist seam sits above the natural waist, there is rarely enough fabric to lengthen it. If the shoulders are far too narrow, the sleeve and armhole would need rebuilding. Recognising these early saves you from accepting a job you will fail.

takeaways: Ease is garment measurement minus body measurement at the same place.
Pulling lines mean tight, bagging folds mean loose, diagonal lines point to the cause.
Keep wearing ease; remove design ease only when the client chooses a closer style.
Write precise amounts on the job card, not vague instructions.

activity.title: Practice task: an ease check on your own clothes
steps: Take your own bust, waist and hip measurements and write them down.
Choose two of your garments, one fitted and one loose, and measure each flat at bust, waist and hip, doubling the flat width.
Calculate the ease at each point for both garments.
Wear each garment in front of a mirror and note any drag lines, with their direction.
Write one sentence per garment: what change, if any, would improve the fit.
activity.evidence: A page with your measurements, the ease table for two garments, and two mirror photos with the drag lines circled or described.

lessons.title: Running an alteration fitting: pinning, chalking and recording
objectives: Prepare a client and a garment for an efficient fitting
Pin out excess and mark new lines accurately on the right side of the garment
Mark a hem level using a fixed height from the floor
Record every change on a fitting card the client confirms

blocks.text: The fitting is the most important 15 minutes of any alteration job. A good fitting gives you exact marks to sew to. A rushed fitting gives you guesses, and guesses lead to second and third fittings that you cannot charge for. This lesson shows a fitting routine you can repeat with every client, from a single trouser hem to a full gown.

blocks.name: safety-pin
blocks.caption: Pins, chalk and a tape measure are the three tools you use most at every fitting.

blocks.text: Before the client arrives

items: **Kit ready:** fine glass-head or dressmaker's pins in a pincushion, safety pins for heavy fabric, tailor's chalk or a chalk pencil (white and one colour), a tape measure, a hem marker or a metre rule, a full-length mirror and your fitting cards.
**Private space:** a curtained corner or room where she can change. Never ask a client to undress where passers-by or apprentices can see.
**Ask her to bring** the shoes she will wear and the underwear she will wear. A bra with different support or heels of a different height can change a fit by several centimetres.

blocks.title: Respect and consent
blocks.text: Tell the client what you are about to do before you touch her: "I am going to pin at your side seam now." Keep your hands flat on the garment, not the body. If the client is a child, a parent or guardian stays in the room. Clients return to tailors they trust.
The fitting routine

items: Put the garment on the client **right side out**, fully closed, in her event shoes. Let her stand naturally with weight on both feet, arms relaxed.
**Look before you pin.** Walk around her once. Note drag lines, the hem level and where the seams hang.
Ask her to sit, raise her arms and bend slightly. Some garments look perfect standing and pull badly when she sits.
**Pin from the top down:** shoulders first, then bust, waist, hip, and the hem last. Changes higher up can change the length lower down.
Pin out excess **evenly on both sides** unless her body is clearly uneven. Pin parallel to the seam, pinching the same amount on left and right.
Mark the hem: measure a fixed height from the floor all round, putting a pin every 8 to 10 cm.
Let her look in the mirror and agree. Then remove the garment carefully so the pins stay in.

blocks.title: Fitting order, top to bottom
items: Shoulders and neckline
Bust and armholes
Waist
Hips and seat
Hem last
blocks.caption: Working from the top down stops a change at the shoulder from spoiling a hem you already marked.

blocks.text: Marking a level hem

Floors and bodies are not perfectly level, so do not simply fold up the same amount all round. Instead, decide the finished length at the centre front, then measure that height from the floor. Keep the ruler upright and move around the client, marking the same height every 8 to 10 cm while she stands still. You move, she does not.

blocks.title: Worked example: marking and cutting a trouser hem
blocks.context: For example, Tunde brings work trousers that drag on the floor. He wears them with the leather shoes he has on. The current finished inside-leg length is 82 cm and the hem allowance turned up inside is 4 cm.
steps: With his shoes on, you fold the trousers up until the hem just touches the top of the shoe at the front with a slight break. You pin there and measure the new finished inside leg: 76 cm.
Shortening amount = 82 - 76 = 6 cm.
You unpick the old hem. The leg now measures 82 + 4 = 86 cm from crotch seam to raw edge.
You keep a 4 cm hem allowance, so the cut line is 76 + 4 = 80 cm from the crotch seam. You cut off 86 - 80 = 6 cm.
You chalk a line 76 cm from the crotch seam as the new fold, check both legs measure the same, then neaten and hem.
blocks.result: Both legs finish at 76 cm with the same 4 cm hem allowance. Because you kept the allowance the same, the amount cut off equals the amount shortened: 6 cm.

blocks.text: The fitting card
Write every change as a number and a place, not a word. Read the card back to the client and ask her to confirm. Many alterers send a photo of the card on WhatsApp so the client has a record too.

head: Area
Change agreed
Notes
rows: Take in 14 cm total, taper to 0 at bust and hip
Use side seams and back darts
Shorten 6 cm, finished at 76 cm inside leg

blocks.title: Pins and children
blocks.text: Count pins out and back into the cushion. A pin left in a garment can scratch a client, and dropped pins on the floor are a danger to children and bare feet. Sweep the fitting area with a magnet after every session.

takeaways: Fit in the event shoes and underwear, right side out, standing naturally.
Look, then test movement, then pin from the top down with the hem last.
Mark hems at a fixed height from the floor, not by folding an equal amount.
Record numbers and places on a fitting card the client confirms.

activity.title: Practice task: a full mock fitting
steps: Ask a friend or relative to wear a skirt or dress that is a little long or loose.
Prepare your kit and a fitting card before she changes.
Follow the fitting routine: look, test movement, pin from the top down.
Mark the hem at a fixed height from the floor with pins every 8 to 10 cm.
Fill in the fitting card with numbers and read it back to her.
activity.evidence: A photo of the pinned garment on the person (with permission) and a photo of the completed fitting card.

lessons.title: Proportion, line and colour: advising clients on what to change
objectives: Use vertical and horizontal lines to explain how an alteration changes a look
Advise on hem and waist placement in a respectful, body-neutral way
Choose thread and trims that match or contrast using the colour wheel
Say no, kindly and clearly, when an alteration will not give the result a client wants

blocks.text: Clients often ask alterers for style advice: "Should I shorten it?", "Will it look better tighter?". Good advice turns a small job into a loyal client. This lesson gives you three simple tools for that advice: **line**, **proportion** and **colour**. You will use them to explain what an alteration will do to the look, so the client chooses with open eyes.

blocks.name: fashion-photoshoot
blocks.alt: A person posing while being photographed in an outfit
blocks.caption: Line, proportion and colour decide how a finished outfit looks in photos and in person.

blocks.text: Line: where the eye travels

The eye follows lines in clothing. **Vertical lines** (front plackets, princess seams, long V-necklines, a single colour from neck to hem) lead the eye up and down, so the outfit looks longer. **Horizontal lines** (a hem, a waist seam, a wide belt, a band of contrast fabric) stop the eye and draw attention to that spot. An alteration moves lines. When you shorten a skirt you move a horizontal line; when you take in a waist you make the waist line more visible.

items: A hem that ends at the **narrowest part** of the leg (just below the knee, or above the ankle) usually looks lighter than a hem that ends at the widest part of the calf.
A waist seam that sits on the client's **natural waist** looks balanced. A waist seam that sits too low or too high makes the bodice look short or long.
Removing a wide contrast band, or replacing it with a narrow piping, can make a gown look longer without changing its length.

blocks.text: Proportion: dividing the body

Many stylists use a simple guide: outfits divided roughly into one-third and two-thirds look more pleasing than outfits cut exactly in half. A short blouse over a long skirt, or a long top over slim trousers, follows this idea. It is a guide, not a rule, and culture matters: a classic iro and buba has its own balance that clients know and love. Use proportion to explain choices, never to criticise a body.

blocks.title: Talk about the garment, not the body
blocks.text: Many books group bodies into shapes such as pear, apple, hourglass or rectangle. These labels can be useful in your head, but avoid saying them to clients. Instead say what the garment will do: "Ending the hem here shows the slimmest part of the leg", not "Because your calves are big".

blocks.title: What a change does to the look
items: Vertical emphasis
Horizontal emphasis
blocks.caption: Vertical lines lengthen the look; horizontal lines draw the eye to where they sit.

blocks.text: Colour: matching thread and trims

In alterations, colour matters most in small choices: thread, zip, lining, piping or a replacement button. On the traditional painter's colour wheel the **complementary** pairs are red and green, yellow and purple, blue and orange. Complements placed side by side look bold and strong. **Analogous** colours, the neighbours on the wheel such as blue, blue-green and green, look calm and harmonious.

head: Job
Matching choice
Contrast choice
rows: Navy thread, or one shade darker
Gold or tan denim thread to match the original
Piping on a green ankara neckline
Orange or red picked from the print
Replacement zip on a cream lace gown

blocks.title: Check colour in daylight
blocks.text: Fluorescent tubes and LED bulbs change how colours look. Hold the thread spool against the garment by a window or at the door before you choose. If you cannot find an exact match, a shade slightly darker usually hides better than one lighter.

blocks.title: Worked example: advising on a skirt length
blocks.context: For example, Grace, a teacher in Ibadan, brings a straight ankara skirt that ends 4 cm above her ankle bone. She asks you to shorten it to the knee because she wants it to look "modern". The skirt is a narrow pencil style with a 20 cm back slit.
steps: You measure: knee length would remove about 40 cm, and the 20 cm slit would disappear completely.
You explain that a narrow skirt at knee length needs a walking slit or vent of its own, otherwise she cannot take a full step. A new 12 to 15 cm slit would have to be made.
You offer two options: (a) knee length with a new back slit, or (b) a midi length ending just below the widest part of the calf, keeping about half of the existing slit.
She tries on the skirt pinned at both lengths and looks in the mirror from the side.
blocks.result: Grace chooses the midi length. You record "shorten 18 cm, keep slit, re-finish slit top". Because she saw both options pinned, she is confident, and she does not come back unhappy.

blocks.text: When to say no

Some requests will not give the result the client imagines. A dress that is far too small cannot become comfortable if the seams hold only 1 cm of allowance. A cheap polyester gown may show old needle holes when let out. Satin and some silks mark permanently where stitches are removed. Say so before you start, show her the seam allowance or the fabric, and offer a realistic option. An honest no keeps your reputation; a failed job damages it.

takeaways: Alterations move lines: hems and waists are horizontal lines the eye stops on.
Use one-third to two-thirds proportions as a guide, never as a judgement on a body.
Match thread one shade darker if you cannot find an exact colour; check in daylight.
Pin options on the client so she sees the result before you cut.

activity.title: Practice task: two-option styling advice
steps: Choose a skirt or dress you or a relative own that could be shortened or taken in.
Pin it at two different lengths or fits, one at a time, and take a side and front photo of each.
Write two sentences explaining what each option does to line and proportion.
Choose a thread colour for the job in daylight and note which colour you chose and why.
activity.evidence: Four photos (two options, front and side) and a short note with your advice and thread choice.

quiz.q: A client's waist is 78 cm and her dress measures 92 cm at the waist. How much ease is there at the waist?
quiz.explain: Ease is garment minus body: 92 - 78 = 14 cm.

quiz.q: You see soft, deep vertical folds hanging at the back waist of a fitted dress. What do they usually mean?
options: There is too much width at the back waist
quiz.explain: Bagging folds that hang down mean extra fabric. Tight areas show fine pulling lines instead.

quiz.q: During a fitting, in what order should you pin a dress that needs shoulder, waist and hem changes?
quiz.explain: Work from the top down. Raising a shoulder or taking in a waist can change where the hem falls, so the hem is marked last.

quiz.q: Trousers have a finished inside leg of 80 cm and a 4 cm hem allowance. The client wants 75 cm and you keep the same allowance. How much do you cut off after unpicking the hem?
quiz.explain: Raw length is 80 + 4 = 84 cm. New cut line is 75 + 4 = 79 cm. 84 - 79 = 5 cm, the same as the shortening amount.

quiz.q: You cannot find an exact thread match for navy trousers. What is usually the best choice?
options: White so you can see the stitches
Black or a navy one shade darker
quiz.explain: A slightly darker shade hides better than a lighter one, and it should be checked in daylight.

quiz.q: A client asks you to take in her kaftan until it is close-fitting. What should you do first?
options: Check whether she wants a different style, because removing design ease changes the garment
Take out all the extra width immediately
quiz.explain: A kaftan's looseness is design ease. Clarify the look she wants and test that she can still sit and move before removing it.

modules.title: Reading a Garment Before You Alter It
modules.overview: A garment can only be changed as far as its construction allows. This module teaches you to inspect seams, darts and allowances to work out how much a garment can be let out or taken in, then applies that thinking to two areas clients often want changed: necklines and sleeves.

lessons.title: Seam allowances, darts and the letting-out calculation
objectives: Inspect a garment and record the usable allowance in each seam
Use the rule that each seam line moved changes the circumference by twice that amount
Calculate whether a garment can be let out enough before accepting the job
Spot fabrics and finishes that will show old stitching after letting out

blocks.text: Taking in is almost always possible: you can sew a seam deeper as long as the style allows. **Letting out is limited** by how much fabric is hidden inside the seams. Before you accept a letting-out job, turn the garment inside out and do a seam inventory. Ten minutes of measuring saves you from promising a size the garment can never reach.

blocks.name: straight-ruler
blocks.caption: A short ruler or seam gauge lets you measure each seam allowance quickly and accurately.

blocks.text: What you are looking for inside

items: **Seam allowance** is the fabric between the stitching line and the cut edge. Home sewing patterns commonly use 1.5 cm. Ready-made clothes often use 1 cm or less, especially on overlocked seams. Tailored trousers and some gowns are made with wider allowances at the centre back so they can be let out.
**Darts** are stitched folds that shape fabric over the bust, waist or hips. A dart can be let out by sewing it narrower, which gives back some of its intake.
**Seam finish.** An overlocked (serged) seam is usually trimmed narrow, so there is little to let out. Pressed-open seams with neatened edges often have more.
**Hidden extras:** a deep hem, a deep facing, or a wide centre-back seam can all give extra fabric.

blocks.title: Leave a safe seam
blocks.text: You cannot use the whole allowance. After letting out, leave at least about 1 cm of fabric beyond the new stitching on woven fabric, and more on fabric that frays easily such as loosely woven linen or some lace. A seam with only a few millimetres left will pull apart.
The doubling rule

Every seam joins two layers of fabric. When you move the stitching line 1 cm outwards on a seam, **each** of the two panels gains 1 cm, so the circumference grows by 2 cm. A skirt has two side seams, so moving both side seams out by 1 cm adds 4 cm in total. The same rule works for taking in: move both side seams in by 1 cm and the skirt loses 4 cm.

blocks.title: How one seam move adds up
items: Total change around body
Two side seams
Two layers per seam
Distance you move the stitching
blocks.caption: Distance moved, times two layers, times number of seams gives the total change in circumference.

blocks.title: Worked example: can this skirt be let out enough?
blocks.context: For example, Bisi brings a lined ankara pencil skirt she wore before having her baby. Her hip is now 102 cm. The skirt hip measures 101 cm. She wants to sit comfortably at church, so you agree at least 5 cm of hip ease, a target of 107 cm.
steps: Extra needed = 107 - 101 = 6 cm.
Side seams: allowance 2 cm each edge, keep 1 cm safe, so 1 cm usable per edge. Two side seams give 1 x 2 x 2 = 4 cm.
Centre-back seam with zip: allowance 1.5 cm, keep 1 cm, so 0.5 cm usable per edge. One seam gives 0.5 x 2 x 1 = 1 cm.
Total possible = 4 + 1 = 5 cm. New hip = 101 + 5 = 106 cm. Ease = 106 - 102 = 4 cm.
The lining must be let out by the same amounts, so you check its seams too: they have the same allowance.
blocks.result: You can reach 106 cm, not 107 cm. You tell Bisi honestly: the skirt will fit with 4 cm of ease, a little snug when sitting. She can accept that, or you can insert matching side panels from her leftover fabric. You do not promise 107 cm.

blocks.text: Will the old stitching show?

When you move a seam outwards, the old stitching line becomes part of the visible garment. On many cottons and ankara prints the needle holes close after washing and pressing. On some fabrics they never disappear.

items: **Satin, taffeta, silk and coated fabrics:** needle holes stay visible. Test by unpicking 2 cm at the bottom of a seam and pressing.
**Denim and dark cottons:** the area inside the seam has faded less, so a darker stripe can show along the old line.
**Lace:** let out only within the lining or along a motif edge; lace seams are often overlapped and trimmed.
**Stretch knits:** old stitching can leave a permanent wavy line.

blocks.title: Test before you promise
blocks.text: If you are unsure, unpick a small section inside a hem or at the lower end of a seam, press it with a pressing cloth, and show the client the mark in daylight. Let her decide whether she accepts it before you go further.

blocks.title: Seam ripper safety
blocks.text: Point the seam ripper away from your body and your other hand. Cut stitches every few centimetres rather than pushing the ripper along the seam, which can slice the fabric itself. Keep rippers and scissors closed and out of children's reach.

takeaways: Letting out is limited by the hidden seam allowance; always do a seam inventory first.
Moving one seam by 1 cm changes the circumference by 2 cm.
Leave at least about 1 cm of safe seam allowance after letting out.
Test fabrics like satin and denim for marks before promising a result.

activity.title: Practice task: a seam inventory
steps: Choose one skirt, dress or pair of trousers and turn it inside out.
Measure and record the allowance at each side seam, the centre back, the darts and the hem.
Work out the maximum the garment could be let out at the waist and hip, leaving 1 cm safe.
Write down which seams you would use and whether any old stitching might show.
activity.evidence: A seam inventory sheet with measurements, your letting-out calculation and a photo of the inside of the garment.

lessons.title: Neckline alterations: lowering, reshaping and re-facing
objectives: Mark a new neckline symmetrically on the client and on the garment
Check that a changed neckline still goes over the head or keeps its opening
Cut and attach a new facing or bias binding to finish the new edge
Prevent stretching and gaping with staystitching and understitching

blocks.text: Clients ask to change necklines more often than you might expect: a round neck that feels tight in the heat, a high neck that does not suit a necklace for an event, or a neckline that gapes. Reshaping a neckline is an alteration that changes the style, so it must be done carefully. Once you cut, the fabric is gone.

blocks.name: womans-clothes
blocks.caption: The neckline is the first thing people see, so a reshaped edge must lie flat and be perfectly even.

blocks.text: What can and cannot be done

head: Request
Usually possible?
What it involves
rows: Cut a new curve, new or reshaped facing
Change round to V or square
Cut new shape, facing cut to match, clip corners
Fabric is gone; only by adding a yoke, panel or lace insert
Small dart hidden under the facing, or take in at the shoulder seam
Cut slightly lower and wider, or add a small opening

blocks.text: Step by step: lowering a round neckline

items: **Mark on the client.** With the garment on, place a pin at the new centre-front depth. Ask her to wear the bra she will wear and check that straps and the bra top will be covered.
**Transfer to the garment.** Lay it flat, fold it in half at centre front, and chalk the new curve on one half. Cut both layers together through the fold so both sides match exactly.
Before cutting, **mark a seam allowance**: the chalk line is the finished edge, so cut about 1 cm outside it for the facing seam.
**Staystitch** about 1 cm from the new raw edge, sewing from shoulder towards centre front on each side. This single line of stitching stops the curved bias edge from stretching.
Unpick and remove the old facing. Use it as a guide to cut a new facing that follows the new curve, about 5 to 6 cm deep, with interfacing if the original had it.

Sew the facing right sides together along the neckline, trim and clip the curve every 1 to 1.5 cm, then **understitch**: stitch the facing to the seam allowances close to the seam so the facing rolls inside and does not show.
Press, then tack the facing down at shoulder seams by hand.

blocks.title: Neckline checks before handover
items: Both sides symmetrical
Bra straps covered
Goes over the head
Facing does not roll out
No stretching at curve
blocks.caption: Check these five points with the client wearing the garment before you finish.

blocks.text: Will it go over the head?

A garment without a zip or button opening must pass over the head. Measure around the client's head over her hair or wrap, around the widest point, and measure the neckline edge on the garment. In woven fabric with no stretch, the neckline opening must be at least as big as the head measurement or she cannot get it on. If you are making a neckline smaller, for example by adding a lace insert to raise it, you may need to add a short back opening with a button and loop.

blocks.title: Worked example: a V-neck for an event blouse
blocks.context: For example, Amaka has a plain round-neck silk-look polyester blouse with a back zip. She wants a V-neck to show a gold pendant at her sister's wedding. The pendant hangs 18 cm below the base of her throat.
steps: At the fitting you pin the V point 20 cm below the base of the throat, so the pendant sits 2 cm above the point. You check from the side that the bra is not visible.
On the flat blouse, you chalk straight lines from the V point to where the old curve meets each shoulder seam, so the neck width at the shoulder stays the same and the shoulders still sit correctly.
You staystitch 1 cm inside the chalk lines before cutting, and stitch the V point with short stitches for strength.
You cut a new V-shaped facing 5 cm deep from matching lining fabric with light fusible interfacing.

After sewing the facing, you clip exactly into the V point up to, but not through, the stitching, then turn, understitch as far as you can reach and press with a pressing cloth on a low iron setting suitable for polyester.
blocks.result: The V sits flat, the point is sharp, and the pendant is framed. Because the back zip already gives an opening, you did not need to check head size, but you note it on the card for reference.

blocks.title: Iron temperature
blocks.text: Synthetic fabrics like polyester and nylon can melt or go shiny under a hot iron. Always test the iron on a seam allowance first, use a pressing cloth, and switch the iron off and stand it upright when you walk away. Keep the cord where nobody can trip or pull it down.

Gaping is the other common neckline complaint, especially on V-necks and wrap tops. Small gaping of about 1 cm can often be removed with a tiny dart under the facing at the edge, hidden on the inside. Larger gaping usually comes from the shoulders being too wide or too long, and is better solved by taking in at the shoulder seam, which you will meet in the dress lesson.

takeaways: Necklines can be lowered or reshaped easily, but raising one needs an added panel.
Cut both sides at once on the fold so the new neckline is symmetrical.
Staystitch the new edge before handling it; understitch the facing so it stays inside.
Check bra coverage and head size before you cut.

activity.title: Practice task: reshape a neckline on an old top
steps: Choose an old woven top or make a simple practice piece from scrap fabric with a round neck and facing.
Mark and cut a new V or scoop neckline on the fold, 1 cm outside your finished line.
Staystitch, cut a new facing, sew, clip, understitch and press.
Check symmetry by folding the top in half at centre front.
activity.evidence: Before and after photos, and a close-up of the inside showing the understitching.

lessons.title: Sleeve alterations: shortening, narrowing and restyling
objectives: Shorten plain-hemmed and cuffed sleeves while keeping the original finish
Narrow a wide sleeve along the underarm seam using the doubling rule
Check that a narrowed sleeve still lets the hand and arm move freely
Recognise sleeve jobs that need more work than the client expects

blocks.text: Sleeves are a frequent request: too long on a ready-made shirt, too wide on a lace blouse, or simply out of style. Some sleeve jobs are quick. Others, such as shortening a sleeve with a buttoned cuff, take far more time than clients realise. Knowing the difference helps you price and schedule properly.

blocks.name: coat
blocks.caption: Sleeve length is checked with the arm relaxed and bent, not stretched straight out.

blocks.text: Measuring sleeve length correctly

Ask the client to stand with arms relaxed at her sides. For a long sleeve, the finished edge usually sits at the wrist bone or just below it. Then ask her to bend her elbow and reach forward: the sleeve rises, and if it now rides far up the arm it was too short already. For jackets worn over shirts, many tailors leave a little of the shirt cuff showing, often around 1 cm. Pin the new length on both arms, because arms are not always the same length.
Three ways to shorten

head: Sleeve type
Method
Watch out for
rows: Unpick or cut, re-hem at the new length
Taper the seam if the sleeve narrows to the wrist, so the new hem is not too tight
Shirt sleeve with cuff and placket
Remove the cuff, cut from the sleeve bottom, re-pleat and re-attach the cuff
The placket gets shorter; check the cuff still opens enough for the hand
Sleeve with lace or beaded edge
Remove the decorative edge, shorten, re-apply the same edge
Allow time to unpick and re-sew the trim by hand

blocks.title: Original finish counts
blocks.text: Clients notice when a cuff or decorative edge does not look like the original. Unpick slowly, keep every piece of trim in a labelled bag, and photograph the original edge before you start so you can copy the pleats, buttons and stitching exactly.
Narrowing a sleeve

Most sleeves have one seam, under the arm. That seam has two layers, so the doubling rule applies: moving the stitching in by 1 cm narrows the sleeve by 2 cm all round. Narrowing is usually tapered: more at the upper arm or forearm, and a smooth line into the armhole so the underarm does not become tight.

blocks.title: Narrowing a sleeve
items: Pin on client, both arms
Measure arm and sleeve
Halve the reduction
Chalk a smooth taper
Test hand and elbow
blocks.caption: Halve the total reduction because the single underarm seam has two layers.

blocks.title: Worked example: narrowing wide blouse sleeves
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma has a cotton blouse with wide, straight sleeves that catch on things when she cooks. Her upper arm measures 32 cm. The sleeve measures 44 cm around at the upper arm and 30 cm at the wrist edge. She wants the sleeves slimmer but still comfortable.
steps: Agreed upper-arm width with ease: 37 cm. Reduction = 44 - 37 = 7 cm. Distance to move the stitching = 7 / 2 = 3.5 cm.
Agreed wrist width: 27 cm. Reduction = 30 - 27 = 3 cm. Distance to move the stitching = 3 / 2 = 1.5 cm.

You chalk a new line 3.5 cm inside the old seam at upper-arm level and 1.5 cm inside at the wrist, joining them with a smooth line, and curve back to 0 cm at the underarm point so the armhole stays the same.
You check that her hand passes through: she makes her hand narrow by tucking the thumb in, and her hand measures 21 cm around at that point, well under the 27 cm wrist width.
You tack the new seam first, she tries it on, bends her elbow and lifts her arms, and only then do you sew and neaten it.
blocks.result: The sleeve is 37 cm at the upper arm and 27 cm at the wrist. It no longer catches on pot handles, and she can still move freely.

blocks.title: Do not change the armhole by accident
blocks.text: If you carry a narrowing line into the armhole seam, you make the armhole smaller and the whole sleeve will pull when she lifts her arm. Always curve your new line back to the original seam just below the underarm point.
Restyling a sleeve

items: **Long to three-quarter or elbow length:** quick if the sleeve has a plain hem. Check the new hem width fits around the forearm or elbow, which is wider than the wrist.
**Removing puffiness at the cap:** reduce the gathers at the top of the sleeve and re-set the sleeve. This takes time and skill and should be priced as a bigger job.
**Removing sleeves completely:** the armhole must then be finished with a facing or bias binding, and may need to be raised slightly at the underarm so the bra does not show.

blocks.text: Always pin and try both sleeves. Bodies are rarely perfectly symmetrical, and a difference of 1 cm in sleeve length between left and right arms is common. Write left and right separately on the job card when they differ.

takeaways: Check sleeve length with arms relaxed and with the elbow bent.
Cuffed sleeves take much longer to shorten than plain-hemmed ones; price them accordingly.
A single underarm seam means the stitching moves half of the total reduction.
Curve narrowing lines back into the original seam before the armhole.

activity.title: Practice task: narrow a sleeve with a taper
steps: Choose a blouse or shirt with a wide sleeve, or a practice sleeve cut from scrap fabric.
Measure the sleeve at upper arm and wrist and decide the new widths.
Calculate how far to move the stitching at each point.
Chalk the new line, tack, try on, adjust, then sew and neaten.
Measure the finished sleeve to confirm your numbers.
activity.evidence: Your calculation, a photo of the chalked line, and a photo of the finished sleeve with a tape measure showing the new width.

quiz.q: You move the stitching on both side seams of a skirt 1.5 cm outwards. How much bigger does the skirt get around the body?
quiz.explain: 1.5 cm x 2 layers x 2 seams = 6 cm.

quiz.q: A dress has 1.5 cm allowance on each side seam edge and you want to leave 1 cm safe. What is the maximum you can let it out using both side seams?
quiz.explain: Usable per edge is 1.5 - 1 = 0.5 cm. 0.5 x 2 layers x 2 seams = 2 cm.

quiz.q: A client wants her round neckline raised by 4 cm. What is the honest answer?
options: The fabric is gone; it can only be raised by adding a panel, yoke or lace insert
quiz.explain: Once a neckline is cut, there is no fabric above it. Raising it needs added fabric.

quiz.q: A sleeve measures 40 cm at the upper arm and the client wants 34 cm. How far in do you move the underarm seam at that level?
quiz.explain: The total reduction is 6 cm; the single seam has two layers, so move it 6 / 2 = 3 cm.

quiz.q: Why do you staystitch a newly cut neckline before attaching the facing?
options: To stop the curved edge stretching out of shape
To make it easier to unpick
quiz.explain: Curved edges are partly on the bias and stretch easily. Staystitching holds the shape.

quiz.q: You are about to let out a satin gown. What should you do before promising the client a result?
options: Unpick a small hidden section, press it and show her whether the needle holes remain
quiz.explain: Satin often keeps needle marks. Testing a hidden area lets the client decide with the facts.

modules.title: Core Alterations: Bodices, Waists, Trousers, Skirts and Gowns
modules.overview: This is the heart of the course: the alterations clients ask for every week. You will take in and let out bodices using side seams, darts and the zip seam, reshape trousers and skirts at the waist, seat and leg, and plan a full gown alteration with linings and an event deadline.

lessons.title: Taking in and letting out bodices: side seams, darts and the zip
objectives: Share a waist reduction between side seams and darts so the shape stays balanced
Work around a zip in a side seam or centre-back seam
Match a bodice change to the skirt at a waist seam
Tack and test before sewing permanently

blocks.text: Taking in a bodice is the alteration you will do most often on dresses, blouses and gown tops. The beginner's mistake is to take all the extra out at the side seams. That pulls the side seams forward or back, flattens the bust shape and can make darts point to the wrong place. A professional result **shares** the reduction between several seams and darts so the garment keeps its original shape, only smaller.

blocks.name: dress
blocks.caption: Bodice alterations share the change between side seams and darts so the dress keeps its shape.

blocks.text: Where the reduction can come from

head: Place
How it removes width
Best for
rows: Each seam moved 1 cm removes 2 cm
General reduction at waist, bust and hip
Stitching each dart leg 0.5 cm further in adds 1 cm to the dart's intake
Shaping the waist without moving the side seams
Each seam moved 1 cm removes 2 cm
Close shaping over the bust and waist on fitted gowns
Back waist hollows, sway back, extra back width

blocks.title: What is dart intake?
blocks.text: The intake is the full width of fabric a dart folds away at its widest point. If a dart is 3 cm wide at the waist and you stitch each leg 0.5 cm further towards the centre, the dart becomes 4 cm wide: 1 cm more is removed. Keep the dart point in the same place, or move it only slightly, so the shaping still aims at the bust or hip.
Working with the zip

Most fitted dresses close with a zip in the centre back or the left side seam. You have three choices. **Take in the other seams only**, leaving the zip alone: quickest, fine for small changes. **Take in the zip seam above and below the zip**, tapering to the zip: rarely neat. **Remove the zip, take in the seam and re-insert the zip**: the correct method when the zip seam must change by more than a few millimetres. An invisible zip must be re-sewn with an invisible zip foot close to the coils.

blocks.title: Choosing where to take in
items: Small change, no zip seam
Small change, darts plus sides
Zip seam re-set needed
Rebuild or refuse
axes: Need to keep shape (low to high)
blocks.caption: The bigger the change and the more shaped the garment, the more seams and darts must share it.

blocks.title: Worked example: taking in a lined dress with a waist seam
blocks.context: For example, Zainab, a nurse in Abuja, has lost weight and wants her lined ankara dress for a staff party in two weeks. The dress has a waist seam, two back waist darts, a side zip on the left and a gathered skirt. Bodice waist: 86 cm. Her waist: 76 cm. She wants about 4 cm of ease, so the target is 80 cm.
steps: Reduction needed at the waist = 86 - 80 = 6 cm.

Right side seam and left zip seam: you move each 1 cm in at the waist, tapering to 0 at the underarm. Two seams x 2 layers x 1 cm = 4 cm. The left zip is removed and re-set because it sits in a seam you are changing.
Two back darts: you increase each dart's intake by 1 cm (0.5 cm further in on each leg). 2 darts x 1 cm = 2 cm.
Total removed = 4 + 2 = 6 cm. New bodice waist = 86 - 6 = 80 cm.
The skirt waist edge must also become 80 cm so the waist seam matches. You unpick the waist seam, pull up the gathers by 6 cm more, and re-join.
The lining is altered by the same amounts, so it does not pull or bag inside.
blocks.result: The bodice and skirt both measure 80 cm at the waist seam, the side seams still hang straight, and the darts still point at the bust. You tack everything first and she approves it at a second fitting before you sew.

blocks.text: Letting out a bodice

Letting out follows the same logic in reverse, limited by the seam inventory from Module 2. Darts can be sewn narrower, which gives back part of their intake. Side seams can be let out only as far as the allowance allows. If a bodice is tight across the bust only, letting out the side seams near the bust and the side bust darts slightly is often enough. If it is tight everywhere, check whether the dress has enough allowance before you accept the job.

items: Pin or chalk the new stitching lines on the inside with the garment inside out, using the fitting card numbers.
Tack (long hand stitches or the longest machine stitch) along the new lines.
Fit again. Look for side seams swinging, darts pointing wrongly, and pulling at the zip.
Sew the final seams with a normal stitch length, then unpick the old stitching and tacking.
Trim excess seam allowance only on a take-in, never below about 1.5 cm, so the garment can be let out again later.
Neaten the seam edges and press seams open or to the back as the original was.

blocks.title: Leave room for the future
blocks.text: Clients' bodies change with pregnancy, illness, age and seasons. When you take in, do not trim seam allowances to almost nothing. Leaving 1.5 to 2 cm lets you or another tailor let the garment out again later, and clients appreciate it when you tell them.

blocks.title: Machine safety
blocks.text: Keep fingers at least a finger's width away from the needle, never sew over pins (pull them out just before the needle reaches them), and switch the machine off at the wall before changing the needle, the foot or oiling it. Unplug the iron and machine when you leave the room.

takeaways: Share a reduction between side seams and darts to keep the original shape.
Increasing each dart leg by 0.5 cm adds 1 cm to the dart's intake.
If the bodice changes at a waist seam, the skirt must change by the same amount.
Tack and fit before sewing, and leave 1.5 to 2 cm of allowance for future letting out.

activity.title: Practice task: plan and tack a bodice take-in
steps: Choose a dress or blouse that is loose at the waist.
Measure the garment waist and decide a target with suitable ease.
Plan how much each side seam and dart will remove so the total matches.
Tack the new lines, try it on, adjust, then sew one side permanently.
activity.evidence: A short plan showing the reduction shared between seams and darts, with the sum checked, plus before and after photos.

lessons.title: Trousers and skirts: waistbands, seat seams, tapering and original hems
objectives: Take in or let out trousers at the centre-back seam through the waistband
Taper a trouser leg evenly using the inseam and outseam
Shorten jeans while keeping the original hem
Adjust a skirt waistband without spoiling its shape

blocks.text: Trousers and skirts bring in steady weekly work: school trousers, office trousers, jeans, and skirts that need a smaller waist. These garments have a waistband, a zip fly or side zip, and often pockets, so you must plan where to make the change without disturbing these parts.

blocks.name: jeans
blocks.caption: Jeans and trousers are the most frequent alteration jobs: waists, tapering and hems.

blocks.text: Trouser waist: the centre-back route

Many men's and some women's tailored trousers are made with a **split waistband** joined at the centre back and a **wide centre-back seam allowance**, often 2 to 4 cm, specifically so they can be altered. This is the easiest route for waist and seat changes because you do not touch the zip fly or the pockets.

items: Unpick the belt loop at the centre back, then the waistband lining and the waistband seam for about 8 to 10 cm on each side of the centre back.
Chalk the new centre-back line. To take in 4 cm in total, move the line 2 cm in at the waist, tapering smoothly to the original seam in the seat curve, about two-thirds of the way down the seat.
Sew the new seam continuously through the waistband and down the seat seam, so the waistband and trousers stay in one line.
Press the seam open, re-close the waistband lining by hand or machine, and re-attach the belt loop.
Try on: check that the back does not pull under the seat when she sits.

blocks.title: Jeans are different
blocks.text: Most jeans have a one-piece waistband and a flat-felled seat seam with two rows of topstitching. Taking in jeans at the back usually means removing the waistband centre section and re-topstitching to match, which takes much longer. Price and schedule jeans waist jobs as a bigger task.
Tapering a trouser leg

A trouser leg has two seams: the inseam (inside leg) and the outseam (outside leg). To keep the crease and the leg hanging straight, take the reduction **equally from both seams**. With two seams and two layers each, move each seam by one quarter of the total reduction at that point.

blocks.title: Tapering a trouser leg
items: Pin leg on client
Measure knee and hem
Divide reduction by four
Chalk both seams equally
Blend into thigh
blocks.caption: Splitting the change equally between inseam and outseam keeps the crease centred.

blocks.title: Worked example: tapering wide office trousers
blocks.context: For example, Chika wants her wide-leg office trousers slimmer. The leg measures 50 cm around at the knee and 46 cm at the hem. She wants 46 cm at the knee and 38 cm at the hem, and the thigh unchanged.
steps: Knee reduction = 50 - 46 = 4 cm. Each seam moves 4 / 4 = 1 cm.
Hem reduction = 46 - 38 = 8 cm. Each seam moves 8 / 4 = 2 cm.
Check: 2 seams x 2 layers x 2 cm = 8 cm at the hem, and 2 seams x 2 layers x 1 cm = 4 cm at the knee.
You chalk the new lines 2 cm in at the hem and 1 cm in at the knee on both seams, then blend smoothly back to the original seams at mid-thigh.
You check that her foot passes through: her heel-to-instep measurement is 31 cm, well under the 38 cm hem, so she can still put the trousers on easily.
blocks.result: Both legs measure 46 cm at the knee and 38 cm at the hem, the crease stays centred, and both legs are cut identically by folding them together to trim.

blocks.text: Shortening jeans and keeping the original hem

Clients often want jeans shortened but love the faded, factory-stitched hem. The **original hem method** keeps it. You fold the leg up to make a tuck that removes the length, sew close to the old hem, then fold the hem back down.

items: Mark the new length on the client in her usual shoes. Suppose she wants 5 cm shorter.
Turn the leg right side out and fold the hem up by half the amount: 5 / 2 = 2.5 cm. A fold of 2.5 cm uses up 5 cm of length because it has two layers.
Pin evenly all round, measuring 2.5 cm from the top edge of the original hem band to the fold.
Using a zipper foot and denim thread or a strong polyester thread matched to the denim, sew all round just below the bottom edge of the original hem band.
Trim the excess inside to about 1 cm, neaten with overlock or zigzag, then fold the original hem down and press. Topstitch close to the seam on the leg if you want the tuck to stay flat.

blocks.text: Skirt waists and waistbands

For a skirt with a waistband, take in at the side seams or darts below the band, then shorten the waistband by the same total amount and re-attach it. On a skirt with a facing instead of a band, take in the facing seams at the same places as the skirt seams so the facing lies flat. For elastic waists, it is usually faster to open the casing at a seam, shorten the elastic and re-close it.

blocks.title: Change the band, not just the skirt
blocks.text: If you take 4 cm out of the skirt but leave the waistband the same length, the skirt will be eased or gathered into the band and look puckered. The band must be shortened by exactly the amount you took from the skirt top edge.

takeaways: Tailored trousers are designed to be altered at the centre-back seam and split waistband.
Taper legs equally on inseam and outseam: each seam moves a quarter of the total.
For an original-hem shortening, fold up half the amount you want to remove.
Shorten a skirt waistband by the same amount you remove from the skirt.

activity.title: Practice task: an original hem on jeans
steps: Find an old pair of jeans or denim scraps with a factory hem.
Decide a shortening amount and fold up half of it all round, measuring as you pin.
Sew below the original hem band with a zipper foot, trim and neaten.
Fold down, press and compare both legs for equal length.
activity.evidence: A photo of the finished hem from the outside, a photo of the inside seam, and a note of your measurements.

lessons.title: Gown and occasion-wear alterations: order of work, linings and deadlines
objectives: Assess a gown fully and list every alteration in the correct order
Raise shoulders and adjust the bodice without spoiling the armhole
Shorten a lined or lace-edged gown hem correctly
Plan fittings and sewing time backwards from the event date

blocks.text: Wedding guests, bridesmaids and aso-ebi groups bring gowns that must be perfect on one fixed date. Gowns carry linings, lace, beads and sometimes boning, and they are expensive. This is high-value alteration work, but it also carries the most risk. A clear assessment, the right order of work and a written plan keep you and the client safe.

blocks.name: spiral-calendar-pad
blocks.caption: Occasion-wear alterations are planned backwards from the event date.

blocks.text: Assess everything first

items: Construction: lining or not, boning in the bodice, type of zip, where the seams and darts are.
Decoration: lace motifs, beads, sequins or stones near any seam you will change.
Fabric: does it mark when unpicked? Does it fray? Is it stretch?
Fit on the client in her event shoes and underwear, with every problem listed on the fitting card.
Existing damage such as a broken zip pull, missing beads or stains, written down and shown to the client before you accept the gown.

blocks.title: Record damage at intake
blocks.text: Photograph any stain, pull, missing bead or broken part in front of the client when you receive the gown, and note it on the job card. Without this record, a client may believe the damage happened in your workshop.
Order of work

blocks.title: Gown alteration order
items: Shoulders and straps
Bust and bodice
Waist and hips
Zip re-set
Hem and lining last
blocks.caption: Each step can change the length below it, so the hem is always finished last.

blocks.text: **Shoulders first.** If a gown is too long in the bodice, the bust shaping sits too low and the waist drops. Taking up the shoulder seams lifts the whole bodice. A 1.5 cm shoulder take-up lifts the bust shaping and the waistline by about 1.5 cm. It also raises the underarm and makes the armhole smaller, so check that the armhole does not cut into her arm afterwards. On a gown with sleeves, the sleeve may need to be unpicked and re-set.

**Bodice and waist next**, sharing the reduction between seams and darts as in lesson 3.1. On boned bodices, the boning channels sit on the seams. You must remove the boning from any channel you change, alter the seam, then re-insert boning cut to the new length with its ends tipped or covered so they do not poke through.
Hems on gowns

items: **Lined gowns:** shorten the outer gown and the lining separately. The lining is usually finished a little shorter than the gown, commonly about 2.5 cm, so it never peeps out below the hem.
**Lace hems with a scalloped edge:** do not cut the scallop off. Remove the lace border, shorten the gown from the top of the border area, then re-apply the border by hand along its motifs.
**Beaded hems:** remove beads in the seam path and save them in a labelled container. Sew them back on after stitching.
**Full or circular skirts:** let them hang for a day before marking the hem, because bias areas drop.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning an aso-ebi gown alteration
blocks.context: For example, Kemi brings a lined lace aso-ebi gown on a Monday for a wedding on Saturday in 12 days. It needs shoulders raised 1.5 cm, the bodice taken in 4 cm, and the hem shortened 8 cm, with a scalloped lace border. You estimate the work time for each task.
steps: Shoulders and re-setting the armhole edge: 45 minutes. Bodice take-in on side seams and darts, outer and lining: 90 minutes. Zip removal and re-set: 40 minutes.
Hem: remove the lace border 40 minutes, shorten the gown and lining 40 minutes, re-apply the border by hand 120 minutes.
Pressing and final check: 25 minutes.
Total = 45 + 90 + 40 + 40 + 40 + 120 + 25 = 400 minutes, which is 6 hours 40 minutes of work.

You plan: fitting 1 today; shoulders and bodice tacked by Thursday; fitting 2 on Friday; hem marked at fitting 2 and finished by the following Wednesday; final fitting and collection on Thursday, two days before the wedding.
blocks.result: Kemi has a written plan with two fittings and a collection two days before the event, which leaves time for any last small fix. You enter 6 hours 40 minutes of work in your weekly schedule so you do not accept too many other jobs.

blocks.title: Never schedule collection for the event day
blocks.text: Aim to finish occasion wear at least two days before the event. If anything goes wrong, from a power cut to a client's change of shoes, you still have time to fix it without panic.

blocks.title: Pressing lace and beads
blocks.text: Press lace and beaded gowns from the wrong side on a padded surface such as a folded towel, with a pressing cloth and a low to medium iron. Direct heat can melt plastic beads and sequins and flatten raised lace.

takeaways: Assess and photograph the gown, including existing damage, before accepting it.
Work from shoulders to hem; the hem and lining are always last.
Lining is finished a little shorter than the gown so it never shows.
Plan backwards from the event and finish at least two days early.

activity.title: Practice task: a gown alteration plan
steps: Choose an occasion dress you or a relative own, or use the worked example details with a new event date.
List every alteration in the correct order with a time estimate for each.
Add up the total time and check the sum.
Write a calendar plan with fitting dates and a collection date two days before the event.
activity.evidence: A written plan with the time estimates, the checked total, and the fitting and collection dates.

quiz.q: A bodice must lose 8 cm at the waist. You move both side seams in by 1.5 cm. How much must the darts remove?
quiz.explain: Side seams remove 1.5 x 2 x 2 = 6 cm. 8 - 6 = 2 cm must come from the darts.

quiz.q: You take 6 cm out of a bodice that is joined to a skirt at a waist seam. What else must you do?
options: Reduce the skirt's top edge by 6 cm so the waist seam matches
quiz.explain: Both pieces meet at the waist seam, so the skirt top edge must change by the same amount.

quiz.q: A trouser leg must lose 12 cm at the hem, shared equally between inseam and outseam. How far do you move each seam?
quiz.explain: Two seams with two layers each: 12 / 4 = 3 cm per seam.

quiz.q: To shorten jeans by 6 cm while keeping the original hem, how deep a fold do you make?
quiz.explain: A fold has two layers, so a 3 cm fold removes 6 cm of length.

quiz.q: A gown needs shoulders raised, waist taken in and hem shortened. Which do you finish last?
quiz.explain: Changes higher up can change the length, so the hem is marked and finished last.

quiz.q: A wedding is on Saturday. When should the gown ideally be ready for collection?
options: By Thursday, at least two days before
quiz.explain: Finishing two days early leaves time to fix any last problem calmly.

modules.title: Restyling: Giving Old Garments a New Life
modules.overview: Restyling goes beyond fitting: you change the style of a garment the client already owns. This module teaches you to judge whether a garment is worth remaking, to calculate whether there is enough fabric, and to carry out two complete restyle projects using alteration skills from earlier modules.

lessons.title: Remake or not? Assessing a garment and checking fabric yield
objectives: Assess an old garment's fabric, seams and condition before agreeing a restyle
Measure usable fabric areas and check that new pattern pieces fit inside them
Explain grain and why pieces must be cut on the same grain as the original
Agree a written restyle brief with a sketch and an honest risk note

blocks.text: Clients bring sentimental and valuable garments for restyling: a mother's lace iro and buba, a wedding guest gown worn once, a husband's old kaftan, a wrapper that is still beautiful but no longer fashionable. Restyling reuses good fabric and gives the client something new without buying new cloth. It also takes longer than a normal alteration, and the fabric is limited to what is already there. Assessment is everything.

blocks.name: eco-conscious
blocks.alt: A person making an eco-friendly choice
blocks.caption: Restyling reuses good fabric that would otherwise sit unused in a wardrobe.

blocks.text: The assessment checklist

blocks.title: Is it worth remaking?
items: Fabric strong, not thin
No fading at folds
Enough usable area
Client loves the fabric
Time fits the budget
blocks.caption: If any of these fails, discuss it with the client before agreeing the job.

items: **Fabric strength.** Hold the fabric up to light and pull gently on the bias. Thin, weak or rotting fabric, especially around underarms and collars, will tear when re-sewn.

**Fading and marks.** Old garments fade unevenly. The inside of seams, the area under a collar and the inside of hems are often darker than the rest. Plan pieces so that faded and unfaded areas do not sit side by side.
**Stains and holes.** Mark them with chalk on the outside so you cut around them.
**Construction.** Is the garment glued, fused or heavily embroidered? Embroidered areas cannot be cut through without spoiling the design.

blocks.title: Grain matters
blocks.text: The **lengthwise grain** runs parallel to the selvedge and is the strongest, most stable direction. In an existing garment, the grain usually runs from shoulder to hem. When you cut a new piece, place its grainline parallel to the old garment's lengthwise grain. A piece cut off-grain will twist and hang badly, even if it is the right size.
Taking the garment apart

items: Photograph the garment front and back before you start.
Unpick seams rather than cutting along them; you gain the seam allowances as usable fabric.
Press each piece flat with steam (if the fabric allows) to remove creases and old stitching lines.
Label each piece with chalk on the wrong side: front, back, sleeve, and an arrow showing the lengthwise grain.
Measure each piece's usable rectangle, avoiding stains, holes and faded lines, and write it down.

blocks.title: Worked example: will an old kaftan make an A-line skirt?
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi brings her late father's cotton kaftan and wants an A-line skirt from it to keep his memory close. After unpicking and pressing, the front and back body panels each give a clean rectangle 70 cm wide and 100 cm long, with the grain running down the length. Each sleeve gives 50 cm by 55 cm.
steps: Her hip is 100 cm. Your skirt pattern has a front and a back piece, each 58 cm wide at the widest point (hem) and 65 cm long, including seam and hem allowances.
Front piece: 58 cm fits within 70 cm width, and 65 cm fits within 100 cm length, with the grain matching. It fits.
Back piece: the same check on the back panel. It fits. Leftover strip on each panel: 70 - 58 = 12 cm wide and 100 - 65 = 35 cm long below the piece.
The skirt needs a waist facing. The front facing is 36 cm long and the back facing 36 cm, each 6 cm deep. Both fit across a sleeve rectangle 50 cm wide.
You chalk a small embroidered motif from the kaftan's neckline as a patch for the skirt pocket, so a recognisable part of his garment shows.
blocks.result: All pieces fit with fabric to spare. You write a brief: A-line skirt, side zip, facing from sleeves, neckline embroidery reused as a pocket patch. You note the risk honestly: the fabric is old, so you will reinforce the seams with a neat overlock or zigzag finish.

blocks.text: The restyle brief

Because restyling changes the style, always agree a short written brief: a simple sketch (even on paper with a biro), what will be kept, what will change, the fittings, and the collection date. Photograph the sketch and send it to the client on WhatsApp. If the client is grieving or emotionally attached to the garment, take extra care to explain what will be cut before you cut it.

head: Brief item
Example entry
rows: Men's cotton kaftan, cream with brown embroidery
A-line skirt, knee length, side zip, faced waist
Old fabric; slight fading near old seams
One fitting at tacking stage, collection in 10 days

blocks.title: Never cut the only copy without consent
blocks.text: A restyle cannot be undone. Get the client's agreement to the sketch and the cutting plan in writing, even if only by a WhatsApp message saying "Yes, go ahead". Keep that message.

takeaways: Check fabric strength, fading, marks and construction before agreeing a restyle.
Unpick rather than cut, press, label pieces with their grain and measure usable rectangles.
Every new piece must fit inside a usable area with the grain running the same way.
Agree a written brief and sketch; restyles cannot be undone.

activity.title: Practice task: a fabric yield check
steps: Choose an old garment you are willing to take apart.
Unpick it, press each piece and measure the usable rectangles.
Choose a simple new item (skirt, top, bag or head wrap) and list the size of each pattern piece.
Check each piece fits inside a rectangle with the grain matching, and write a short restyle brief with a sketch.
activity.evidence: Photos of the pressed pieces with measurements written beside them, and your restyle brief with sketch.

lessons.title: Two restyle projects: a shirt into a fitted blouse, a maxi dress gains sleeves
objectives: Plan a restyle that combines several alterations in the right order
Turn an oversized shirt into a fitted blouse using side seams and darts
Shorten a maxi dress and use the cut-off fabric to add sleeves
Explain honestly the limits of each restyle to the client

blocks.text: This lesson brings together everything from Modules 1 to 3 in two complete projects. Each one is popular with clients and makes good portfolio pieces. Read both, then choose one to complete as your practice task.

blocks.name: t-shirt
blocks.caption: An oversized shirt can be reshaped into a fitted blouse with side seams, darts and shorter sleeves.

blocks.text: Project 1: an oversized shirt into a fitted blouse

A large men's cotton shirt in a good print or a crisp plain colour can become a fitted women's blouse. The work is mainly taking in, with back darts added for shape, and shortening the sleeves. The important limit is the **shoulders**: a men's shirt shoulder will sit beyond her shoulder bone. You either accept a soft, dropped-shoulder look, which suits casual styles, or remove the sleeves, narrow the shoulders and re-set the sleeves, which is advanced work and must be priced as such.

blocks.title: Worked example: shaping the shirt
blocks.context: For example, Aisha wants her brother's old shirt as a fitted blouse to wear with jeans. Shirt chest: 120 cm, shirt waist: 118 cm. Her bust: 96 cm, waist: 82 cm. She chooses a dropped-shoulder casual look, 8 cm of bust ease and 10 cm of waist ease.
steps: Target bust = 96 + 8 = 104 cm. Reduction = 120 - 104 = 16 cm. Side seams: 16 / 4 = 4 cm moved in on each side seam at bust level.
Target waist = 82 + 10 = 92 cm. Reduction = 118 - 92 = 26 cm.
Side seams at the waist: moved in 5 cm each, removing 5 x 2 x 2 = 20 cm.
Two new back waist darts, each with 3 cm intake: 2 x 3 = 6 cm. Total = 20 + 6 = 26 cm.
The sleeves are taken in along the underarm seam in a continuous line with the side seam, then shortened to elbow length with a new hem.
blocks.result: The blouse measures 104 cm at the bust and 92 cm at the waist, with soft dropped shoulders. Because the side seam and sleeve seam are sewn in one continuous line from hem to sleeve end, you can do both in one pass on most shirts.

items: Unpick the shirt hem at the side seams for about 5 cm so you can re-hem neatly afterwards.
Turn inside out, chalk the new side seam and sleeve line in one continuous curve, tack and fit.
Sew the darts and seams, trim and neaten (most shirts use flat-felled seams; a neat overlock or French seam is fine for the new seam).
Shorten the sleeves and re-hem, then re-close the shirt hem at the sides.
Press and photograph before and after for your portfolio, with the client's permission.

blocks.text: Project 2: shorten a maxi dress and add sleeves

Many clients have a sleeveless maxi dress they want to wear to church or the office, where they prefer covered arms. If the dress is longer than she needs, the fabric cut from the hem can become cap sleeves in exactly the same fabric. The sleeves will match perfectly because they come from the same cloth.

blocks.title: Maxi dress to sleeved midi
items: Mark new length
Cut strip from hem
Cut sleeves on grain
Finish armholes, set sleeves
Hem the dress
blocks.caption: The fabric removed from the hem becomes the new sleeves.

blocks.title: Worked example: is the hem strip big enough for sleeves?
blocks.context: For example, Funke's sleeveless maxi dress is 145 cm long from shoulder to finished hem. She wants it 120 cm long with short cap sleeves. The hem circumference is 180 cm. Each cap sleeve pattern piece is 46 cm wide and 14 cm tall, including seam and hem allowances. Her armhole measures 44 cm around.
steps: New finished length 120 cm plus a 3 cm hem allowance gives a cut line at 120 + 3 = 123 cm from the shoulder.
The strip below the cut line is 145 - 123 = 22 cm tall (above the old hem fold) and 180 cm around.
The sleeve is 14 cm tall, which fits in 22 cm. You place the sleeve so its centre line runs from shoulder to hem of the dress, keeping the lengthwise grain the same as the dress.
Two sleeves need 46 + 46 = 92 cm of width, which fits within the 180 cm strip, leaving 88 cm.
The sleeve width of 46 cm is 2 cm more than the 44 cm armhole: that small extra is ease, eased into the armhole around the top of the shoulder.
blocks.result: Both sleeves fit with 88 cm of strip left over, enough for a matching head wrap or a fabric belt. You agree the sleeve shape with Funke using a paper pattern pinned on the dress before cutting.

blocks.title: Check before you cut
blocks.text: Do not cut the dress hem until you have pinned a paper sleeve pattern onto the dress at the shoulder and the client has approved the look and the new length. Once cut, the length cannot be returned.

takeaways: A restyle combines several alterations; plan them in order from top to hem.
A men's shirt keeps wide shoulders unless you re-set the sleeves, which is advanced work.
Fabric cut from a long hem can become sleeves, belts or head wraps in matching cloth.
Pin a paper pattern and get approval before cutting anything you cannot replace.

activity.title: Practice task: complete one restyle project
steps: Choose Project 1 or Project 2 and find a suitable garment.
Write the measurements and calculations, checking every sum.
Tack and fit before sewing permanently.
Finish, press and take before and after photos in daylight from the same angle.
activity.evidence: Your calculation sheet, a tacked-fitting photo, and before and after photos of the finished restyle.

quiz.q: An unpicked panel gives a usable rectangle 60 cm wide and 90 cm long. Which pattern piece fits with the grain running down the length?
quiz.explain: Only 55 x 85 fits inside 60 x 90 without turning the piece off-grain.

quiz.q: Why should you unpick old seams instead of cutting along them when restyling?
options: You gain the seam allowances as usable fabric
quiz.explain: Unpicking keeps the fabric inside the seams, which adds to the usable area.

quiz.q: A shirt measures 116 cm at the chest and the target is 100 cm. How far do you move each side seam in at bust level?
quiz.explain: The reduction is 16 cm; two side seams with two layers each: 16 / 4 = 4 cm.

quiz.q: A maxi dress is 150 cm long. The new finished length is 118 cm with a 4 cm hem allowance. How tall is the strip you cut off?
quiz.explain: Cut line is 118 + 4 = 122 cm. Strip = 150 - 122 = 28 cm.

quiz.q: What is the main limit when turning a large men's shirt into a fitted women's blouse?
options: The wide shoulders, unless the sleeves are re-set
quiz.explain: Taking in side seams does not narrow the shoulders. Either accept a dropped shoulder or re-set the sleeves.

quiz.q: A client wants her late mother's lace gown restyled. What must happen before you cut?
options: Cut a test piece from the front
Agree a sketch and cutting plan, and get her written yes, even on WhatsApp
quiz.explain: Restyles cannot be undone. A written agreement protects the client and you.

modules.title: Running and Pricing an Alteration Service
modules.overview: Alterations are many small jobs with short deadlines, so they need their own system. This module shows you how to take in, tag and schedule garments so nothing is lost or late, and how to price each alteration from the time it really takes and its difficulty.

lessons.title: The alteration counter: intake, tagging, scheduling and collection
objectives: Receive a garment with a numbered tag, a job slip and photos of its condition
Estimate weekly capacity in minutes and decide whether to accept new jobs
Set clear turnaround times, including a rush option
Handle uncollected garments and client privacy fairly

blocks.text: An alteration business may have 20 or 30 garments in the workshop at once, many of them looking alike: five pairs of black trousers, three aso-ebi gowns in the same lace. One mixed-up garment can lose a client and cost you the price of the item. A simple counter system prevents this and lets you promise dates you can keep.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: A numbered tag on every garment is the simplest way to stop mix-ups.

blocks.text: Intake: five things for every garment

items: **Tag it.** Pin or tie a numbered tag to the garment (for example 0127). Write the same number on the job slip and in your job book or phone note.
**Write the job slip.** Client name and phone number, garment description, every alteration with exact amounts from the fitting card, price agreed, deposit paid, and collection date.
**Photograph the garment** front and back, and close-ups of any existing stains, pulls, missing buttons or beads. Show the client and note them on the slip.
**Empty the pockets** in front of the client and hand back anything you find.
**Give the client her copy** of the slip, or a WhatsApp photo of it, and keep yours.

blocks.title: Group similar jobs
blocks.text: Hang garments by job type: all hems together, all waist jobs together, gowns separately. Doing all the trouser hems in one session saves time because you change thread and machine settings less often.

blocks.title: The alteration job cycle
items: Intake and tag
Fitting and pinning
Sewing and pressing
Quality check
Collection and payment
blocks.caption: Every garment goes round the same cycle, and its tag number follows it at every step.

blocks.text: How much work can you accept?

Time your jobs for two or three weeks, from picking up the garment to hanging it finished. Write the minutes on each job slip. You will soon know your real times. Then compare the total minutes of work booked for the week with the minutes you actually have for sewing, after fittings, cooking, children, church and travel to the market for supplies.

blocks.title: Worked example: can she take one more gown this week?
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat runs alterations from a room in her house in Ilorin. She can sew about 5 hours a day, 6 days a week, but she keeps half of that time free for fittings, collections, buying supplies and the jobs that always take longer than planned. This week she has booked 10 trouser hems at 30 minutes each, 4 waist take-ins at 75 minutes each, 2 zip replacements at 45 minutes each and 1 gown at 240 minutes.
steps: Available sewing time: 5 hours x 6 days = 30 hours. Half kept free, so 15 hours = 900 minutes for planned work.
Booked: hems 10 x 30 = 300 minutes; waists 4 x 75 = 300 minutes; zips 2 x 45 = 90 minutes; gown 240 minutes.
Total booked = 300 + 300 + 90 + 240 = 930 minutes, or 15 hours 30 minutes.
She is already 30 minutes over her 900-minute planning limit before any new job.
blocks.result: Rukayat does not promise another gown this week. She offers the new client a date next week, or a rush slot only if she moves her own rest day, at a rush price.

blocks.text: Turnaround and rush jobs

head: Service
Example standard turnaround
Notes
rows: Rush same or next day if space allows
Waist, taper, sleeve or zip job
At least two fittings, finish two days before event

blocks.text: These turnaround times are only examples; set yours from your own timed jobs. Always add a rush charge when a job pushes other work aside, because it costs you time with other clients or your own family.
Collection, uncollected garments and privacy

items: **Check at collection:** let the client try on fitted alterations, or at least check the measurement with her. Fix small issues on the spot if you can.
**Reminders:** send a polite WhatsApp message when the item is ready, and again after a week.
