**Uncollected items:** write your rule on the job slip at intake, for example that items not collected within 60 days after two reminders may be donated or sold to cover the cost. Only use a rule the client agreed to in writing, and keep the reminders as proof.

**Privacy:** client measurements and phone numbers are personal information. Keep your job book out of sight, do not share client photos without permission, and never post a client's body measurements or her garment on a status without asking.

blocks.title: Payment scams
blocks.text: Never release a garment against a screenshot of a transfer alone. Fake transfer alerts and edited screenshots are common. Confirm that the money has actually arrived in your bank or wallet app (for example Moniepoint, OPay or your bank's app) before handing over.

takeaways: Tag, slip, photograph, empty pockets and give the client a copy at every intake.
Plan work in minutes and keep spare time for fittings and surprises.
Set turnaround times from your own timed jobs and charge for rush work.
Confirm payment in your own app before releasing any garment.

activity.title: Practice task: build your counter kit
steps: Make 20 numbered tags from card and string or safety pins.
Design a one-page job slip with all the fields from this lesson, including your uncollected-items rule.
Time three alteration jobs from start to finish and write the minutes down.
Work out your weekly planning limit in minutes using your own available hours.
activity.evidence: A photo of your tags and a blank job slip, and a note with three timed jobs and your weekly planning limit.

lessons.title: Pricing alteration jobs by time, difficulty and urgency
objectives: Calculate an hourly rate from your income target, costs and real working hours
Price a job from timed minutes, a difficulty factor and materials
Build a clear alteration price list with starting prices
Take deposits and explain prices to clients with confidence

blocks.text: Many alterers price by guessing or by copying the shop next door. That leads to cheap prices on slow, difficult jobs and arguments when a gown takes four times as long as a hem. A time-based method is fair to you and easy to explain to clients: the price follows the work.

blocks.name: stopwatch
blocks.caption: Timing your jobs is the foundation of fair alteration prices.

blocks.text: Step 1: your hourly rate

Start with what you want to earn in a month, then add your monthly running costs: thread, needles, chalk, zips you keep in stock, electricity or fuel for a generator, phone data and transport to the market. Divide by the hours you can actually sell. Do not count every hour you are in the workshop: fittings, buying supplies, cleaning and messages also take time, so billable hours are fewer than working hours.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting an hourly rate
blocks.context: For example, Esther in Port Harcourt wants to take home about 150,000 naira a month. Her running costs are about 30,000 naira a month. She works 20 days a month and can bill about 5 hours a day. All naira figures here are illustrations only; use your own numbers.
steps: Monthly total needed = 150,000 + 30,000 = 180,000 naira.
Billable hours = 20 days x 5 hours = 100 hours.
Hourly rate = 180,000 / 100 = 1,800 naira an hour, which is 30 naira a minute.
blocks.result: Esther's working rate is 1,800 naira an hour. Every price on her list starts from this number.

blocks.text: Step 2: price each job

**Price = (minutes x rate per minute x difficulty factor) + materials**, then round to a tidy figure. The **difficulty factor** covers risk and skill: delicate fabric, beads, linings, boning, or a garment that is costly to replace. Use 1.0 for simple jobs on easy fabric, and higher factors, such as 1.25 or 1.5, for risky ones. Materials are anything you supply, like a new zip, elastic or interfacing.

blocks.title: Building an alteration price
items: Rounded final price
Plus materials

Minutes times rate

head: Job
Minutes

blocks.text: The table uses Esther's illustration rate. Your times and rate will differ. Notice how the gown hem, which looks like "just a hem" to a client, costs more than ten trouser hems because it takes eight times as long and carries more risk.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a zip replacement with materials
blocks.context: For example, a client brings a skirt with a broken invisible zip. Esther times the job at 50 minutes including unpicking. The fabric is ordinary cotton, so the difficulty factor is 1.0. She supplies a new invisible zip that costs her about 500 naira.
steps: Time cost = 50 x 30 = 1,500 naira.
Difficulty 1.0, so it stays 1,500 naira.
Add materials: 1,500 + 500 = 2,000 naira.
blocks.result: The price is 2,000 naira. If the client wants it the same day and Esther must move another job, she adds her rush charge, for example 50 percent of the labour: 1,500 x 0.5 = 750 naira, making 2,750 naira.

blocks.text: Step 3: price list, deposits and explaining prices

items: **Publish starting prices** ("from 1,000 naira") on a WhatsApp Business catalogue or a printed card, and confirm the final price after the fitting.
**Deposits:** take a deposit on gowns, restyles and any job where you buy materials, for example half the price. Small hems can be paid at collection.
**Explain with time:** "This gown hem takes about four hours because the lace border is sewn back by hand." Clients accept a price more easily when they understand the work.
**Review prices** every few months: re-time your jobs and recheck your costs, especially when fuel, electricity or thread prices change.

blocks.title: Do not discount by guessing
blocks.text: If a client asks for a lower price, offer a lower-cost option rather than the same work for less, for example a machine blind hem instead of a hand-finished one, or a longer turnaround instead of rush.

blocks.title: Keep a simple record
blocks.text: Write every job, its minutes, price and payment method in one notebook or spreadsheet. At the end of each month, add up income and costs. If your real hours per job are higher than your price list assumes, raise the price or speed up your method.

Finally, decide your **re-fix rule** and write it on the price card. For example: small adjustments to your own work are free within seven days of collection if the client brings the garment back with her slip. Changes she asks for later, or a new style, are a new job at the normal price. A clear rule protects your time and makes clients trust you, because they know you stand behind your work.

takeaways: Hourly rate = (income target + monthly costs) / billable hours.
Price = minutes x rate per minute x difficulty factor, plus materials, rounded.
Charge for rush work and take deposits on gowns, restyles and bought materials.
Re-time jobs and review prices every few months.

activity.title: Practice task: your own alteration price list
steps: Write your monthly income target and running costs, and your real billable hours.
Calculate your hourly rate and rate per minute.
Using your timed jobs from lesson 5.1, price at least six common alterations with difficulty factors and materials.
Round the prices and design a simple price card with starting prices and your deposit rule.
activity.evidence: Your rate calculation, a pricing table for six jobs with sums checked, and a photo or screenshot of your price card.

quiz.q: A tailor wants 120,000 naira a month, has 20,000 naira of running costs and 80 billable hours. What is her hourly rate?
Her rate is 30 naira a minute. A beaded sleeve job takes 60 minutes with a difficulty factor of 1.5. What is the time cost before materials?
A client sends a screenshot showing she has transferred the balance and asks to collect her gown. What should you do?
options: Check your own bank or wallet app to confirm the money has arrived first
Keep the gown for a week
Ask her to send the screenshot again
quiz.explain: Screenshots can be faked. Confirm the payment in your own app before releasing any garment.

quiz.q: Her planning limit is 900 minutes a week and she has 860 minutes booked. A new job takes 75 minutes. What is the best response?
options: Offer next week or a rush slot at a rush price
Accept it and skip the second fitting
quiz.explain: 860 + 75 = 935 minutes, over the limit. Offer a later date or a paid rush slot.

quiz.q: Which of these should be done at intake for every garment?
options: Tag it, write a slip, photograph existing damage and empty pockets
Post a photo on your status
quiz.explain: These steps prevent mix-ups and disputes about damage and lost items.

quiz.q: A client asks you to reduce the price of a hand-finished lace hem. What is the better response?
options: Offer a lower-cost option, such as a different finish or a longer turnaround
Do the same work for less
quiz.explain: Offering a cheaper option keeps your rate fair while giving the client a choice.

finalQuiz.q: A client's hip is 100 cm and her skirt measures 104 cm at the hip. How much hip ease does the skirt have?
finalQuiz.explain: Ease is garment minus body: 104 - 100 = 4 cm.

finalQuiz.q: During a fitting, what should the client wear?
options: Any shoes, it does not matter
The shoes and underwear she will wear with the garment
finalQuiz.explain: Shoes change hem length and underwear changes bust and waist fit, so fit in what she will wear.

finalQuiz.q: Which advice about body shape is most professional?
options: Tell her to lose weight first
Describe what the alteration does to the garment's line, not her body
Tell her she is a pear shape
finalQuiz.explain: Talk about the garment's line and proportion. Labels about bodies can hurt and lose clients.

finalQuiz.q: A skirt's side seams each have 2.5 cm allowance per edge and you keep 1 cm safe. How much can it be let out using both side seams?
finalQuiz.explain: Usable per edge is 1.5 cm. 1.5 x 2 layers x 2 seams = 6 cm.

finalQuiz.q: After cutting a new lower neckline, what stops the facing rolling out to the right side?
options: Understitching the facing to the seam allowances
Pressing with a very hot iron
finalQuiz.explain: Understitching holds the seam allowances to the facing so it rolls to the inside.

finalQuiz.q: Narrowing a sleeve, you carry the new seam line straight into the armhole. What will happen?
options: The armhole becomes smaller and the sleeve pulls when she lifts her arm
The sleeve will be more comfortable
finalQuiz.explain: Curve the new line back to the original seam before the underarm to keep the armhole size.

finalQuiz.q: A bodice must lose 10 cm. Side seams are moved in 2 cm each. How much must two back darts remove in total?
finalQuiz.explain: Side seams remove 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cm. 10 - 8 = 2 cm, so each dart's intake grows by 1 cm.

finalQuiz.q: Trousers must lose 6 cm at the hem, shared equally between inseam and outseam. How far do you move each seam?
finalQuiz.explain: 6 cm divided by 4 (two seams, two layers each) = 1.5 cm.

finalQuiz.q: Why is a gown's lining usually finished a little shorter than the gown?
options: So it never shows below the hem
finalQuiz.explain: A slightly shorter lining stays hidden when the client walks and sits.

finalQuiz.q: A maxi dress is 140 cm long. New finished length 115 cm, hem allowance 3 cm. How tall is the cut-off strip?
Her rate is 1,500 naira an hour. A job takes 40 minutes, difficulty 1.0, with a 400 naira zip. What is the price before rounding?
finalQuiz.explain: 1,500 / 60 = 25 naira a minute. 40 x 25 = 1,000, plus 400 = 1,400 naira.

finalQuiz.q: What is the best protection against a dispute about a stain on a client's gown?
options: Photograph and note it on the job slip at intake, in front of her
finalQuiz.explain: A dated photo and slip note show the stain was there before the gown entered your workshop.

capstone.title: Alterations portfolio: three client jobs from fitting to handover
capstone.brief: Complete three real alteration jobs for three different people (one waist or bodice job, one trouser or sleeve job, and one hem or restyle job) and submit a portfolio that shows your fitting cards, calculations, before and after photos, timed minutes, prices and client feedback.
steps: Run a full fitting for each job, record every change on a fitting card and get the client's confirmation.
Do a seam inventory and write the take-in or let-out calculation for each job, checking every sum.
Tag each garment, write a job slip and photograph its condition at intake.
Tack and fit before sewing; complete the alterations in the correct order and press.
Time each job in minutes and calculate its price with your own hourly rate, difficulty factor and materials.
Check the fit with the client at collection and record her feedback.
Write a one-page reflection: what went well, what took longer than expected and how you will change your prices or methods.
evidence: Three completed fitting cards with numbers and places
Three calculation sheets with sums checked
Before and after photos of each garment in daylight from the same angle
Timing and pricing table for the three jobs
Client feedback for each job (message or note)
